note: Teaching text, clarifying questions, inferred constraints and own examples. Inferred, not official. Examples are small generated inputs with outputs from the independent references in oracles.py.

constraints: 1 <= L <= 10, every word has length L
clarifyingQuestions: Do all strings have the same length?
May the chosen strings be reordered freely?
Is the empty selection allowed (answer 0)?
hints: With equal lengths, the word in block i must be the reverse of the word in block m - 1 - i.
Count words; a word w and its reverse r != w form min(count[w], count[r]) pairs.
A palindromic word pairs with itself count // 2 times; one leftover palindromic word may sit in the middle.
invariants: each word entry is used at most once
the chosen blocks read the same in both directions
chooseWhen: Pairing items with mirror partners under multiplicities
tradeoffs: Counting is linear; exhaustive search is only usable for a handful of words
hack2hire:67cf33498f73eb6319edd230.variantLabel: Inferred single variant: equal-length words paired with their reverses

clarifyingQuestions: Is "within 10 minutes" measured between consecutive orders (chaining) or from the first order of a group?
Where do unit prices and tier thresholds come from?
How is a fractional discounted price rounded?
Is the answer a total, a per-group list or a per-fruit breakdown?
hints: Group orders by fruit with a hash map, then sort each fruit's orders by timestamp.
Start a new group whenever the gap to the previous order exceeds 600000.
For a group of two or more orders, find the last tier with minQuantity <= Q by binary search and apply floor(Q * price * (100 - percent) / 100).
invariants: every order belongs to exactly one group
a single-order group pays full price
chooseWhen: Session-style grouping of timestamped events per key
tradeoffs: Sorting per key costs n log n; the pairwise component reference is quadratic
hack2hire:685c61e88515b8a3b59d19f9.variantLabel: Inferred single variant: chained 10-minute purchase groups with tiered discounts

constraints: location and friend names are 1 to 10 letters or digits
clarifyingQuestions: What is asked: who picks up whom, the arrival time, or the meeting point of the two routes?
If both drivers pass a home, who picks the friend up?
How are ties broken?
Can a friend live at a starting location?
hints: Each location has one outgoing road, so a hash map from location to road gives the next step in O(1).
Walk each route from its start and record the arrival time at every location.
For each friend compare the two arrival times (missing = never), then sort each driver's friends by arrival time with input order as tie break.
invariants: arrival times strictly increase along a route
every friend is listed exactly once
chooseWhen: Functional-graph walks with per-node timestamps
tradeoffs: Hash-map walks are linear; repeated road scans are quadratic but trivially correct
hack2hire:68c86e64df5a6365aa774b11.variantLabel: Inferred single variant: assign each friend to the first driver to pass their home

clarifyingQuestions: Are car ids 0-based or 1-based?
Which free car is chosen: the smallest id or the one free longest?
In what order are reservations processed when starts tie?
Is the fleet size limited?
hints: Sort reservations by start time, keeping the input index for ties and for the output.
Before each reservation, release every busy car whose end <= start into a free-id min-heap.
Take the smallest free id, or open a new car; push (end, id) onto the busy heap.
invariants: no two overlapping reservations share a car
the number of cars equals the maximum overlap
chooseWhen: Resource assignment with reuse of the lowest identifier
tradeoffs: Two heaps give n log n; a linear scan over cars is O(n * cars)
hack2hire:69b7856c8a0eeb9897a8d239.variantLabel: Inferred level 1: smallest free car id, unbounded fleet

clarifyingQuestions: Are car ids 0-based or 1-based?
Which free car is chosen: the smallest id or the one free longest?
In what order are reservations processed when starts tie?
Is the fleet size limited?
hints: Seed a free-id min-heap with 1..cars and process reservations by (start, index).
Release busy cars whose end <= start before each reservation.
When the free heap is empty, record -1 and do not occupy anything.
invariants: at most cars reservations are active at once
a rejected reservation never blocks later ones
chooseWhen: Admission control with a fixed resource pool
tradeoffs: A heap of free ids avoids scanning all cars per reservation
hack2hire:69b785888a0eeb9897a8d23b.variantLabel: Inferred level 2: fixed fleet size, rejected reservations get -1

clarifyingQuestions: Is the output a boolean list or a binary string?
Is p guaranteed to be a permutation?
hints: Values 1..k must occupy a window of exactly k positions.
Keep the leftmost and rightmost positions among values 1..k as k grows.
The answer for k is true exactly when right - left + 1 == k.
invariants: left and right bound every position of 1..k
the span never shrinks as k grows
chooseWhen: Checking contiguity of a growing value set
tradeoffs: The span test is linear; window sorting is cubic
hack2hire:69efd6f096981f58ae1f6dcf.variantLabel: Inferred single variant: span of the positions of 1..k

clarifyingQuestions: Can two entries be the same point?
Is the answer a float, the squared distance or a rounded value?
Are coordinates integers?
hints: Sort by x, split at the median and solve both halves.
Points closer than the best distance d across the split lie in a strip of width 2d around the median x.
Sorted by y, each strip point only needs comparing with the next few strip points whose y differs by less than d; use squared integer distances and take one square root at the end.
invariants: best is the minimum squared distance among pairs examined so far
each recursion returns its points sorted by y
chooseWhen: Geometric nearest-pair queries on large point sets
tradeoffs: n log n divide and conquer versus n^2 brute force; a grid hash is simpler but needs care with distribution
hack2hire:690425df4845d25b8e994896.variantLabel: Inferred single variant: classic closest pair by divide and conquer

constraints: each tree has at most 1e4 nodes
level-order lists use null for absent children and have no trailing null
clarifyingQuestions: How are trees encoded?
Do later source trees see sums already added from earlier ones?
Is the result returned in level order with trailing nulls removed?
hints: Decode level-order lists into left/right child index arrays.
Walk a source tree and the result tree together breadth-first, starting at the roots.
At each source node add value + children values to the result node, creating result nodes (value 0) where missing; serialise in level order and trim trailing nulls.
invariants: source trees are read only
every source position exists in the result after its pass
chooseWhen: Overlaying positional data across tree structures
tradeoffs: A paired breadth-first walk is linear; path-string maps are simple but cost O(depth) per node
hack2hire:69c42c3e21f6ab4226965a1f.variantLabel: Inferred single variant: positional merge of neighbor sums into the last tree

clarifyingQuestions: Is a task first done on day 1 or on day intervals[i]?
Do several completions of different tasks on one day all count?
hints: By day d, task i has run floor((d - 1) / intervals[i]) + 1 times.
That total is non-decreasing in d, so binary search the smallest d reaching goal.
Upper bound: the fastest task alone reaches goal by day 1 + (goal - 1) * min(intervals); stop summing as soon as the running total reaches goal.
invariants: the count function is monotone in d
the answer lies between 1 and the single-task bound
chooseWhen: Smallest time to reach a production target with periodic producers
tradeoffs: Binary search is logarithmic in the answer; a heap simulation is linear in goal
hack2hire:6775b4fd0d31dc201f712039.variantLabel: Inferred single variant: binary search on the day count

clarifyingQuestions: What are the method names and signatures?
Can intervals be added after construction?
Are endpoints inclusive?
hints: An interval covers x when it has started (l <= x) and not yet ended (r >= x).
Sort the starts and the ends separately once.
Answer = (number of starts <= x) - (number of ends < x), each found by binary search.
invariants: every interval with l <= x is counted once by the first term
intervals with r < x also have l <= x, so subtracting them is exact
chooseWhen: Static stabbing queries over many intervals
tradeoffs: Two sorted arrays answer in O(log n); a segment tree would also support updates
hack2hire:692fc0f4cd79766b0b3101a0.variantLabel: Inferred single variant: static stabbing counts

clarifyingQuestions: Must the runs appear in the order of arr?
Are runs maximal (separated by at least one "0")?
Can the count exceed 64-bit range?
hints: Let f(i, j) count completions of pattern[i:] using segments arr[j:].
Either pattern[i] becomes "0" (it must not be "1"), or the run arr[j] starts at i: the next arr[j] characters contain no "0" and the character after them is not "1".
Precompute prefix counts of "0" so each run check is O(1); f(L, m) = 1.
invariants: f(i, j) depends only on later positions
each counted string has exactly the runs in arr
chooseWhen: Counting constrained fillings of a pattern
tradeoffs: Memoised DP is polynomial; enumeration doubles with every question mark
hack2hire:67844afb0e1dbb6a0938577f.variantLabel: Inferred single variant: nonogram line counting

clarifyingQuestions: Does "below" include an equal price?
How is a sell order matched?
Are new orders streamed in or are only the initial lists matched?
What is returned: matches, totals or the final book?
hints: Keep resting sells in a min-heap and resting buys in a max-heap.
An incoming buy checks the cheapest sell: if it is <= the buy price, pop and report it.
Otherwise push the incoming order onto its own side and report -1; sells mirror this with the highest buy.
invariants: the heaps hold exactly the unmatched orders
a match never violates either price limit
chooseWhen: Limit order books with price priority
tradeoffs: Heaps give log time per order; sorted lists give linear insertion
hack2hire:678ec4943d1b82777aa24f9a.variantLabel: Inferred single variant: incoming orders against a resting book

constraints: at most 5 tags per datapoint, each 1 to 8 lowercase letters
clarifyingQuestions: Is k a time width or a number of datapoints?
Is the window inclusive at both ends?
Are datapoints sorted by timestamp?
Is one sum returned per datapoint or one overall value?
hints: Filter the datapoints that carry the tag; timestamps stay increasing.
Keep a window [left, right] and a running sum; add each new datapoint.
Advance left while its timestamp is below t - k + 1, subtracting its value, then record the sum.
invariants: the running sum equals the sum of the window
left never moves backwards
chooseWhen: Rolling metrics over time-stamped telemetry
tradeoffs: Two pointers are linear; prefix sums with binary search also work in n log n
hack2hire:696c54fe6b040fa4d120bca7.variantLabel: Inferred level 1: time window of width k

clarifyingQuestions: Is an empty remainder balanced?
Is the smallest index wanted when several work?
hints: Elements before the removed block keep their indices.
Elements after it move left by k, so their parity flips exactly when k is odd.
With prefix sums E and O of even- and odd-index values, compare E_before + (shifted suffix even part) with O_before + (shifted suffix odd part) for each i.
invariants: prefix sums are exact integers below 2**53
i is tried in increasing order
chooseWhen: Removing a block and re-indexing with parity bookkeeping
tradeoffs: Prefix sums give O(n); rebuilding arrays is O(n^2)
hack2hire:68672293a2d59460201f2cae.variantLabel: Inferred single variant: prefix sums with parity shift

constraints: each component 0 to 1e6 without leading zeros
clarifyingQuestions: What does the VersionChecker method look like and is the number of calls limited?
What is returned when no version has the feature?
Are versions compared numerically per component?
Are the versions always given sorted?
hints: The answers are false...false true...true, so the first true is a boundary.
Binary search with lo = 0, hi = n: test the middle and keep the half that contains the boundary.
If lo reaches n, no version supports the feature and the answer is null.
invariants: all indices below lo answer false
all indices at or above hi answer true
chooseWhen: First-bad-version style boundary searches
tradeoffs: Binary search uses O(log n) API calls; a scan uses O(n)
hack2hire:6913fb43fa8a311e42671e69.variantLabel: Inferred level 1: binary search over sorted versions

constraints: each component 0 to 1e6 without leading zeros
supported is monotone in numeric version order
clarifyingQuestions: What does the VersionChecker method look like and is the number of calls limited?
What is returned when no version has the feature?
Are versions compared numerically per component?
Are the versions always given sorted?
hints: String order is wrong for versions ("10.0.0" < "9.0.0" as strings); compare integer components.
Sort indices by the parsed (major, minor, patch) triple.
Binary search the sorted order for the first index whose answer is true.
invariants: the sorted order is strictly increasing numerically
answers along the sorted order are monotone
chooseWhen: Searching semantic versions
tradeoffs: Sorting costs n log n; the numeric minimum over true answers is linear but uses every answer
hack2hire:69141530fa8a311e42671e8f.variantLabel: Inferred level 2: numeric version sort, then binary search

clarifyingQuestions: What are the names and signatures of the query methods?
Do queries return ids or names?
How are score ties ranked?
Does a first vote count as a flip?
hints: Store each (user, article) vote as +1, -1 or absent; the score change is new vote minus old vote.
A flip happens only when the old vote is the opposite non-zero vote; move that article to the front of the user's recent-flip order.
Keep article ids sorted by (-score, id): on a score change remove the id by binary search with the old key and insert it with the new key; the top k is a prefix.
invariants: the sorted array always matches current scores
each user's flip order lists distinct articles
chooseWhen: Voting systems with ranking and per-user activity queries
tradeoffs: A sorted array has cheap queries and O(A) updates; a balanced tree would make updates logarithmic
hack2hire:69334452e8ebbb1c53caf2c4.variantLabel: Inferred single variant: votes, flips and ranking

constraints: total returned cells over a trace <= 1e6
clarifyingQuestions: Is row 0 the top or the bottom of the board?
Is the board returned as characters or strings?
What happens after a player has already won?
How is a winner reported when nobody has won?
hints: Track how many pieces each column holds.
The next piece in column c goes to row rows - 1 - height[c] when height[c] < rows.
Return a fresh copy (new row lists) so later drops cannot change an earlier result.
invariants: height[c] equals the number of non-"0" cells in column c
earlier returned boards are never modified
chooseWhen: Grid games with gravity
tradeoffs: Copying the whole board per call costs rows * cols; returning only the changed cell would be cheaper but is not what is asked
hack2hire:69bdbad91cbff60a929beb23.variantLabel: Inferred level 1: gravity drops returning board copies

constraints: total returned cells over a trace <= 1e6
clarifyingQuestions: Is row 0 the top or the bottom of the board?
Is the board returned as characters or strings?
What happens after a player has already won?
How is a winner reported when nobody has won?
hints: A new line of four must pass through the piece just dropped.
For each of the four directions count equal cells on both sides of the new piece.
If any direction reaches 4 and there is no winner yet, record this color; getWinner returns it or "0".
